bigThing.title: Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
bigThing.description: New York architect Diana Kellogg has renovated her historic Tribeca residence, highlighting materials repurposed from its industrial past. Kellogg and her family have occupied the home on Staple Street for 25 years, which is close to the studio that the architect shares with her filmmaker husband. Diana Kellogg has updated her home gradually over time, while retaining its industrial character The building originally served as cold storage for neighbouring produce distribution facilities, then became a plumber's supply storefront and eventually a residence around 50 years ago. Kellogg has renovated and updated the structure gradually over the years, and when her kids moved out, she decided to undertake a more comprehensive overhaul. Many of the built-in elements are formed from the salvage of the building's freight elevator An old freight elevator was removed and replaced with a space that Kellogg refers to as the Green Room. The glass-wrapped nook is lined with cushioned seating and used for intimate catch-ups over drinks, or private video calls. The kitchen similarly utilises salvaged elements The salvage from the elevator and other elements around the building were repurposed to create structures for the kitchen, bookcases, and a staircase that connects the four levels. "Throughout the house there were old glass and steel doors, and windows and stuff," Kellogg said. "I just moved them around and repurposed them." A space dubbed the Green Room is used for catch-ups and Zoom calls In keeping with the architecture, the decor remains industrial and spare, highlighting key elements like the fireplace and the 25-foot-long chestnut beams that span the ceiling. "It was a massive pain in the neck to strip those, but one of the best decisions we made, because they add so much warmth and character," said Kellogg. A steel staircase connects the home's four levels During the most recent renovation, the upstairs bedrooms with vaulted brick ceilings were reconfigured as neutrally decorated spaces separated by sliding mahogany doors. On the ground floor, the children's former playroom – complete with climbing ropes and a swing – was converted into a comfortable TV room, featuring a large L-shaped sofa and a variety of midcentury furniture pieces. The ground-floor children's playroom was recently converted into a media room Matching those on the level above, Noguchi pendant lights hang from the steel beams that Kellogg added to suspend the "jungle gym". "There's still one climbing rope down there that people think is an art piece, which I love," she said. Read: Crina Arghirescu Rogard adds "eccentric design" to historic penthouse in Tribeca Key artworks include a pair of photographs by Ljubodrag Andric , which he produced to sit either side of the first-floor fireplace and "give the place so much depth and warmth," said Kellogg. Downstairs, the walls are adorned with images of The Rajkumari Ratnavati Girl's School that Kellogg completed in 2021 in India's Thar Desert. Upstairs bedrooms are divided by mahogany sliding doors The roof terrace was relandscaped with planters and a variety of wooden outdoor furniture that forms dining and seating areas with views of a historic bridge between the adjacent buildings. "I really wanted an oasis up there, and to have it be a second living room," said Kellogg. "And there's the fabulous bridge, which we have kind of great views of from our house – which is, in my opinion, better than actually being inside it." The roof terrace was also refurbished with planters and outdoor furniture Many of Tribeca's former industrial buildings are now residential, housing large lofts and penthouses, while others contain galleries and creative spaces. Examples of other homes in the neighbourhood include a penthouse in the American Thread Building updated by Crina Arghirescu Rogard and a loft that Andrea Leung renovated to conceal "secret spaces". The photography is by Andrew Brinka . The post Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials appeared first on Dezeen .

signals.title: How to measure if AI agents actually use your Design System
signals.description: What I learned from Christoph Hellmuth at our AI Jam on September 29 2026 Christoph Hellmuth is Design Engineering Manager for Design Systems at NordVPN . His team builds Aurora. That is the design system behind NordVPN and other Nord Security products. At our AI Jam he showed Open Design System Bench . It is an open source tool that measures how well AI agents follow your design system and gives you a score from 0 to 100. These are my notes from his session. 😱 The AGENTS.md was there and the models still built their own buttons Christoph’s team did what everyone recommends. Aurora ships an AGENTS.md. Then they measured what the models actually did with it. In 41 of 57 guided generations the models hand-rolled buttons, dialogs and toggles instead of using the design system they were told about. That is 72%. “It just invented a button, and honestly, we were quite shocked, because we were thinking, like, yeah, best practices, they work well.” Every model launch comes with a scoreboard like SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench. None of them checks whether an agent uses your Button instead of inventing one. That gap hurts when leadership asks what the 50 to 80 hours of AI readiness work brought. Without a number you only have a feeling. “Cool, so can you prove it? And you… well, we did all these best practices, but not really, and that’s not really what leadership wants to hear.” 🔍 Two tools: a free audit and a behavioral benchmark The static audit reads your repo. It costs nothing and took 5 to 10 seconds in Christoph’s live demo. It checks what you ship for agents such as AGENTS.md, llms.txt, skills and catalog quality. You get a score plus a list of what is missing. The behavioral benchmark lets an agent build real screens with your system in a fresh workspace. Then it grades the result. You can also run the audit against several systems at once. Christoph compared open source systems like Carbon, Primer, Base UI and MUI. Chakra scored highest with 70.5. “In this just static check of 10 seconds, it also gives you basically a to-do list, and you can now go into Jira, create the tickets for the next month.” The audit score is always the optimistic one. Ticking checkboxes is easy. The real score shows up once an agent has to use your system. 📝 Tasks describe intent and never the component The benchmark ships with 10 tasks. One example is a password reset screen. Another is the area where a user cancels a subscription. A task never names a component. Otherwise you only test whether the model can read. You can write your own tasks and weigh the rubric yourself. Christoph’s example: a red destructive cancel button can count for more than a support link. A built-in linter checks your task before you run it. In his demo it failed a task because the prompt mentioned the real export PasswordInput . 📊 What gets graded Each output is scored on six dimensions. The weights come from the README : imports (10%): Only your package, React and local files are imported apiFidelity (25%): No hallucinated components or invented props tokenDiscipline (15%): No raw hex values, arbitrary Tailwind or hardcoded styles a11yStatic (10%): Accessible names, labels and valid ARIA compile (10%): TypeScript compiles judgment (30%): Per-task rubric graded by a separate model By default every task runs 3 times per model. The worst run counts so the score never looks better than what a designer would get on a bad day. The hallucinations Christoph found in Aurora were very specific. Aurora has a heading prop and the model invented a Heading component. Aurora has Text and the model used Typography . It also invented spacing props on Box and Card. “They hand over the AI generated prototype to developers. And they tell you, well, we don’t really have any of these props, or this is an invented component.” 📉 The repo read 20 points better than it behaved Christoph ran the benchmark on Aurora AppKit. The audit gave it 64.8. Six models building with it scored 44.9. Only 10 of 55 guided cells compiled against the published types. The npm run produced about 250 type errors. About 100 of them came from direction="column" on a prop that only takes 'vertical' | 'horizontal' . The uncomfortable part: their own AGENTS.md and DESIGN.md mentioned a cn helper and a bare Radix component that never existed in the codebase. Their docs were teaching the agent some of the traps. 💡 One sentence in the README flipped it Their AGENTS.md told the model what not to use. In the run against the source code 72% of the buttons were still hand-rolled. Then they added one sentence to the README saying the package is installed. In the run against the npm package only 22% were hand-rolled. “Even things you thought, oh, this is useless, like, why should I tell the AI that my design system package is installed? No, it actually makes a difference.” After fixing the findings the audit score went from 64.8 to 82.0. The fixes included exporting the types nobody had exported and generating an llms.txt. He also tested six open models with and without an AGENTS.md. In the session he said adding one file moved the scores by 20 to 30 points. His write-up lists DeepSeek V4 Pro going from 58.7 to 84.8 and Sonnet 5 single-shot going from 51.2 to 75.3. 🛠️ How to run it on your design system The repo supports React and TypeScript libraries plus web components built with Stencil or Lit. Your system can be local source or an npm package. Clone open-design-system-bench Install and set it up: npm install npx tsx src/cli.ts init # wizard asks for package name, location and how you serve it npx tsx src/cli.ts doctor # checks your config and CLI setup npx tsx src/cli.ts extract # builds the component catalog npx tsx src/cli.ts run --profile smoke # 2 cells in about 5 minutes Run the bigger profiles once the smoke test passes. small has 5 cells for weekly checks and full has 90 cells for a quarterly baseline. You do not have to type any of this. Christoph and I both said it in the session: paste the repo link into Claude Code and ask it to install the benchmark and run it against your design system. A full run with Claude Code took him half an hour to an hour. His run with 6 models took about 3 hours. Watch the cost. Through the API a run with the top models can cost a few hundred dollars. A subscription is much cheaper. Christoph’s tip for the report: give it to Claude and ask for a PDF for leadership with an executive summary, the models tested, the results and the costs. 🎨 What about Figma? Vee asked in the Q&A whether you can score Figma and code together. Christoph’s answer: a Figma file alone mostly tests how well the AI uses the Figma MCP. It says little about your design system. His recommendation for the Figma to code workflow is Code Connect. “Honestly, at least from what we’ve seen, CodeConnect is totally worth having for, your Figma to code, workflow.” What I’m taking back to my own work These are my own takeaways and not Christoph’s: Run the free audit first. It takes seconds and gives you a ticket list. Never trust the audit score alone. Aurora lost 20 points once agents had to build with it. Tell the agent what to use and not only what to avoid. Grep your own AGENTS.md for helpers and components that do not exist. Write benchmark tasks the way a designer would brief a screen. Never name the component. Links from the session Open Design System Bench on GitHub Christoph’s write-up with all results Open Design System MCP : an MCP server from Christoph that exposes your real components and tokens to agents so they stop inventing names and props What Does AI-Readiness Mean in Design Systems? by Cristian Morales Design Engineer job in the Aurora team at Nord Security Watch Christoph’s full session and the live demo The recording of this AI Jam is part of the AI Design Systems Conference 2027 ticket. The conference runs online on March 10 and 11 2027 with speakers from Anthropic, OpenAI, Atlassian, Netflix and Yahoo. signals.title: Seven striking buildings that make a statement with red
signals.description: A timber-clad fire station and an arena with a zigzagging facade are among the projects that feature in this roundup of red buildings. Photo by Måns Berg Liden's Brandstation, Sweden, by Kod Arkitekter Stockholm studio Kod Arkitekter used bright red-stained cladding to distinguish this fire station in Liden, Sweden , as a local landmark. Its concrete and glue-laminated timber structure is partially sunken into the site, which was selected for its close proximity to a nearby highway that will help ensure "rapid emergency response". Find out more about Lidens Brandstation › Photo by Fabrice Fouillet Jihlava Municipal Arena, Czech Republic, by Chybík + Krištof A zigzagging facade made up of red aluminium panels was chosen to create a strong civic identity for this ice hockey arena in Jihlava, Czech Republic . Completed by local studio Chybík + Krištof , the 5,650-seat Jihlava Municipal Arena serves as a cultural hub for the city as well as a home for a local ice hockey team – to which the red colour of the facade also nods. Find out more about Jihlava Municipal Arena › Photo by Jasmine Hughes Cucu, Ireland, by Studio Bucky New York practice Studio Bucky used red-stained shingles to create a "sense of personality and wonder" at the off-grid Cucu cabin in rural Westmeath, Ireland . Alongside its red, shingle-clad exterior, the cabin 's tapered form and irregular openings contribute to Studio Bucky's task of creating a unique retreat for cabin rental brand Samsú. Find out more about Cucu › Photo by Alik Usik Prostir Business Hub, Ukraine, by Aranchii Architects Warehouse-like volumes cloaked in bright red metal panels form the Prostir Business Hub on the outskirts of Lviv, Ukraine, completed by local studio Aranchii Architects . Located in the village of Zymna Voda, the 12,000-square-metre logistics hub provides commercial, office and storage spaces organised across a trio of buildings with curved gable roofs. Find out more about Prostir Business Hub › Photo by Madara Kupla House Comet, Latvia, by Gaiss Local architecture studio Gaiss designed this family home in Riga as a contemporary take on a traditional Latvian barn. Complete with a "bold and distinctive" exterior, House Comet is defined by red-painted timber walls and a white corrugated metal roof. Find out more about House Comet › Photo by Iwan Baan William T Cannady Hall for Architecture, US, by Karamuk Kuo A jagged, terracotta and glass extension was added to the Rice School of Architecture in Houston, Texas , by Swiss architecture studio Karamuk Kuo. The two-storey addition encompasses 22,000 square feet (2,044 square metres) and is topped with a distinctive sawtooth roof that "echoes the industrial vocabulary of fabrication spaces". Find out more about William T Cannady Hall for Architecture › Photo by Peter Fabo House With a Red Addition, Czech Republic, by Facha Architekti Prague-based Facha Architekti added a red- corrugated-metal extension to a small family home in the Czech Republic. Housed within a former pigsty, the existing home was expanded to accommodate an additional living space and an adjacent larch terrace that improves connections to the outdoors. Find out more about House With a Red Addition › The post Seven striking buildings that make a statement with red appeared first on Dezeen .

visualFeast.title: Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers
visualFeast.description: Furniture brand Karimoku New Standard has announced the global release of its KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which repurposes upcycled foam from unused ASICS trainers as cushioning for two seating designs. The KNS x ASICS Collaboration uses deadstock and sample footwear from ASICS that would have otherwise been discarded. Karimoku New Standard, a sub-brand of Japanese manufacturer Karimoku , used the same technique that ASICS has utilised for its upcycled Neocurve trainers to create the material for the collaboration. ASICS trainers are crushed to extract EVA foam The ASICS footwear is dismantled, sorted and crushed to extract Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) foam, a flexible, light material commonly used as cushioning for midsoles, outsoles and footbeds. After the foam has been extracted, it is blended with cotton and paired with a three-millimetre condensed foam sheet to create a hybrid structure, according to Karimoku New Standard . The material is then used as cushioning in the brand's Castor Lobby Sofa and Polar Lounge Chair, which also feature an embroidered tag as a symbol of the collaboration. Read: Issey Miyake designs "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers for ASICS The KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which was introduced in Japan earlier this year before the recent global launch, came about after Karimoku New Standard was working on seating for the meeting spaces in ASICS' Tokyo office. "Through rigorous sessions with ASICS – leveraging their expertise in sports science – and a meticulous adjustment process for real-world office use, Karimoku repeatedly prototyped to transform an unfamiliar material like shoe waste into true furniture comfort," Karimoku New Standard said. "This uncompromising, hands-on exploration led to the creation of the innovative hybrid structure," the brand continued. "Beyond merely reusing materials from a sustainability standpoint, it turns them into a functional added value." The Polar Lounge Chair was made using upcycled sneakers Karimoku has previously collaborated with brands including Zaha Hadid Design . ASICS recently released the "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers with fashion brand Issey Miyake and has also designed pastel-coloured trainers with Danish brand Hay . The images are courtesy of Karimoku New Standard. The post Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers appeared first on Dezeen .

Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai
visualFeast.description: A giant spiral staircase guides visitors to the roof of the Shanghai Grand Opera House, which international studio Snøhetta designed to be "as much a civic destination as a performance venue". Located on the Huangpu River waterfront in Shanghai, China, the 146,786-square-metre opera house was conceived as a major cultural landmark that can accommodate a variety of musical performances. Snøhetta has completed the Shanghai Grand Opera House While Snøhetta 's design responds to a highly ambitious brief, the studio said it began the project as it always does, by taking time to examine and understand the specific site and its context, no matter the scale. According to the studio, this helped it to create the desired landmark while ensuring it felt like an extension of the existing public realm, open and accessible to both ticket holders and passersby. It is located on the Huangpu River waterfront "We always begin the same way, regardless of scale: by understanding the context," Snøhetta co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen. "A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of," he reflected. "When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context." Its key feature is a giant spiral staircase Shanghai Grand Opera House's defining feature is its spiral staircase, which dramatically cantilevers at its peak and was intended to emulate everything from an unfolding fan to a dancer or a set of piano keys. It leads directly to the publicly accessible rooftop, which doubles as a stage, an observation deck or simply a meeting point. According to Thorsen, it was integral to making the building feel part of the urban fabric. The staircase has a dramatic cantilever He compared the design to the Oslo Opera House , which the studio completed in 2000, with both designs actively seeking to "reduce thresholds wherever possible". "Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors, and ticketed programs. We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue," Thorsen explained. "People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city," he added. "A successful landmark is not only recognised by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives." The lobby is designed to feel light and open Shanghai Grand Opera House has a radial plan and contains a trio of auditoriums alongside exhibition and education spaces, restaurants and rehearsal and production areas. The facade flits between transparent and opaque finishes, depending on where the studio wanted to provide privacy and openness. For example, expansive glass elements maximise natural light and views in the lobby. The main auditorium has five levels Together, the three auditoriums can accommodate 4,200 people and host a range of performances. The main auditorium, called the Harmony Hall, contains 2,000 seats across its five levels, while the second hall, named the Soar Theatre, is more intimate, with space for 1,200 people. The final auditorium contains 1,000 seats and was constructed as a highly flexible space with adaptive seating and staging, catering to more experimental performances. It is fronted with a large glass facade overlooking the river. "For younger generations especially, that flexibility can help make cultural experiences feel more relevant, accessible, and connected to contemporary life," said Thorsen. Read: Snøhetta's Oslo Opera House was the most significant building of 2007 Shanghai Grand Opera House's material palette is a play of contrasts, with the light-coloured white stone, glass, and timber exterior having a more open feel than the darker, more intimate interiors. Inside, the auditoriums each have a unique aesthetic. The main hall is filled with deep red tones and surfaces, intended to feel as though they are carved from a single block, while lighter wooden materials characterise the other two. At night, the stage towers that project from the building are illuminated, shifting in colour to "animate the roof and the skyline". The smallest performance hall is designed to be adaptive Minimising the building's carbon footprint was a significant challenge due to the building's "scale and complexity", Thorsen said, but this was achieved through measures including passive design strategies. The bright roof reflects sunlight and heat rather than absorbing it, and the public lobby opens towards both the river and the park, allowing for cross-ventilation. A palette of durable materials and an adaptable interior will ensure a long lifespan for the building, while a close connection to public transport minimises dependence on private vehicles. Shanghai Grand Opera House is complete with a landscape design that connects to existing parkland, wetlands and public spaces to support local biodiversity and provide ample public space. The other auditorium accommodates 1,200 guests Snøhetta was founded by Thorsen and Craig Dykers in 1989. It won an international competition to design the opera house in 2016 and developed it with the state-owned firm East China Architectural Design & Research Institute (ECADI) and consultants Theatre Projects and Nagata Acoustics . Other major cultural projects by the studio include the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota and the rippled Glasshouse Theatre in Queensland . The photography is by Yumeng Zhu , Tian Fangfang , Chen Hao and StudioSZ . The post Snøhetta completes landmark opera house in Shanghai appeared first on Dezeen .
